description: Tall tapering corn-cob shaped tower of Khmer-derived form on a stepped terrace, its whole surface encrusted with fine relief.

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Tall tapering tower of rounded corn-cob profile on a high stepped square terrace, vertical bands of stacked receding tiers curving inward to a pointed trident finial, redented corner mouldings running the full height, a small niche with a false door on each face, steep narrow stairs up the terrace on one side Materials: Encrusted mosaic of broken porcelain shards and coloured glass over pale render, gilded trident finial, sun-bleached and lichen-spotted stonework on the terrace, dark rain runs in the vertical mouldings.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: FINAL VERDICT. Overall visual fidelity 0.92. Band table 0.008 / 0.013 of height against the reference; the tier arches the first build omitted are what moved every layer. 18,060/32,000 triangles, 9/24 draw calls, 6/16 materials, 9/32 unique geometries, 3 canvas textures at 4.0 MB.

featureReviews.evidence: Envelope built at exactly 9.00 x 18.00 x 9.00 m (the first build's finial overshot to 18.21), and area-weighted band comparison against the Meshy reference gives mean |delta width| 0.008 and |delta depth| 0.013 of height with every band inside 0.03. The rebuild settled three bands: the tier stack now steps IN from the body (band 6 -0.006 against the first build's +0.037), the body-top arch row is shallow (band 5 +0.005 against +0.030), and the top tenth is finial alone (band 9 +0.019 against +0.068).
featureReviews.notes: The stair is the one asymmetric thing on the prop and it is cut INTO the terrace plan as a notch.

featureReviews.evidence: Seven octagonal tiers from 10.20 to 15.20 m, apothem 1.55 down to 0.62 on a cosine raised to 1.3, each wearing a ring of EIGHT round-headed arches 1.05 of the octagon side wide and 1.38 of the tier tall -- so neighbours interleave and every ring reaches into the tier above -- with a 0.13 m plain stucco rim standing 0.08 m proud of the encrusted field, and a row of four shallow arches over the body top. Closed by a domed cap to 15.90 and a 2.25 m finial.
featureReviews.notes: The first build shipped plain stepped slabs with a lip and recorded the arches as 'below the resolvable band'; they are the tier stack's whole identity at any distance the silhouette can be read from, and the plate at zoom shows nothing else on the tiers. Corner arches at the same radius as face arches are why the cores are octagons rather than the body's redented plan.

featureReviews.evidence: Blind arched door under a POINTED pediment frame rising from its head, on each of four faces from ONE instanced unit; sixteen red pilaster strips, two per re-entrant face, from a four-instance unit at radius zero; a row of four large arches at the body top over the pediments.
featureReviews.notes: The plate's redent corners carry groups of red strips edged with a white chevron; the chevron is not authored. The dark grey water streaks in the re-entrants are carried only by the tile's washes.

featureReviews.evidence: Three notched slabs (upper two narrowed to 4.05 and 3.55 on band 1), a balustrade broken at the stair head, and a twelve-tread flight with raking cheeks -- twenty-two parts in ONE component and ONE draw call. Stone re-authored whiter (#CDBDAD envelope) with lichen coverage halved and joints deepened to 0.50 after the first build read as a flat ochre block against the plate's pale coursed limestone.
featureReviews.notes: check-coplanar reports the prop clean at 0.001 m.

name: Prang
notes: The tall slender Thai prang of the Wat Arun type: rounded corn-cob profile, encrusted porcelain surface, trident finial. It is deliberately a separate asset from a Khmer stone sanctuary even though both descend from the same Khmer tower form, because they read as completely different objects -- this one is tall, slim, pale and encrusted, while the Khmer original is squat, dark sandstone and ruined. Declared at 18 m, well above the building-part category's 8 m prior, which is correct for a riverside prang. No destruction groups: it is static landmark geometry.
